batch_strategy: Select 32 experiments through targeted condition contrasts, follow-up of endpoint anomalies, and structural transfer tests. Freeze the supplied premeasurement predictions unchanged for every selected ID. Prioritize labels that distinguish loading effects, scaffold-dependent solvent response, and independent finish behavior. Use CW distance and quantile spans as secondary evidence: zero V2 lower quantiles and crossed V1 quantiles limit their interpretation as uncertainty.

choices.reason: Measure m127 at 50/1 and 50 ul, below the loading of a3ae677aae8a8faf5786, whose measured endpoints nearly coincide at 35.44/35.52 mL. Together with the selected 150 ul condition, this tests whether that unusual endpoint pattern extends across loading; the current prediction remains appreciably broader at 29.85/42.36.

Measure m127 at 50/1 and 150 ul to bracket the anomalous 100 ul observation a3ae677aae8a8faf5786. Predictions barely change between the selected 50 and 150 ul rows, so this contrast can expose loading dependence that the model currently smooths away.

The 20/1, 100 ul m127 condition provides a fixed-loading ratio contrast to a3ae677aae8a8faf5786. The measured 20/1, 150 ul row ebdeaba52880c7eade16 has early onset but a long finish, making this useful for separating onset curvature, loading effects, and the high-ratio endpoint anomaly.

The m57 50/1, 150 ul observation 63ec73e3341feaaf43ae gave 16.05/16.08 mL despite a much earlier acquisition-time prediction. Measuring 50 ul at the same ratio tests whether this late, nearly coincident endpoint pattern transfers across amount in a scaffold without conventional hydrogen-bonding groups.

Pair m57 at 20/1 and 50 ul with its selected 50/1 condition. Measured 10/1, 50 ul data in 137b5aaf9ecf3d65b7e3 and the anomalous 50/1 result in 63ec73e3341feaaf43ae leave the intervening response unresolved; this label tests the predicted onset shift without assuming a universal solvent-response shape.

Measure m125 at 1/1, 50 ul with 300 ul DCM. The otherwise matched 500 ul DCM observation f4fb5c03b8e8996e75f6 gave 12.49/36.14, while 4c32851430464f0ed684 anchors 100 ul sample with 300 ul DCM. This fills a direct loading-solvent-volume contrast where current predictions are nearly volume-insensitive.

Measure m125 at 2/1, 150 ul with 300 ul DCM against the otherwise matched 500 ul condition facbcedbecb46072b04c. Existing 300 ul observations 5c2bc1d92128a17d996d and c8d43713db33bf820a1d cover lower amounts, so this completes a useful local loading surface and tests whether its large finish differences persist.

Measure m94 at 20/1 and 50 ul below the measured 100 and 150 ul conditions e3a799d0fa90b649a157 and ffffcd6f3b9393846ab4. Recent 668279c54bbf75e86496 had accurate onset but underestimated finish by 7.67 mL at acquisition. This label tests loading transfer within the established late-retention regime.

Complete the m135 10/1 amount series at 100 ul. Measured onset changes from 47.38 mL at 50 ul in f433bc672465387d951a to 34.69 mL at 150 ul in d05a91dc8e32e9edd7d0, whereas their finishes are much closer. The midpoint can teach endpoint-specific loading response.

Measure the sparsely constrained secondary alcohol m60 at 5/1 and 50 ul, predicted at 19.83/32.83. Its measured neat-EA anchor ca6df7e85e3c4bd22b40 does not establish this response. Comparison with the alcohol-family observation bf09d868ed4d68a97b40 and the selected 10/1 point tests structural transfer into a steeper retention region.

Hold m60 sample amount and PE loading conditions fixed while moving from the selected 5/1 to 10/1 condition. The predicted increase to 42.29/71.76 is substantial. This pair tests whether alcohol position and substitution produce a steep response distinct from the measured benzylic alcohol m67 in 2d11f1fe488a0c917ffe.

Fill m74 at 20/1 and 100 ul between measured 10/1 and 50/1 conditions bfaadd073aa5a950f919 and 027bbff1ac308c5dd7a1. Recent f72a0e7948a50ed09024 showed an acquisition-time finish underestimate at 5/1. This interior label constrains curvature for a brominated diester rather than relying on endpoint interpolation.

Measure m166 at 20/1 and 100 ul, paired with the phenyl analogue m167 under the same recorded loading conditions. The measured m166 finish was underestimated in 0fca9e0134ba9700cc0c and 20acd2ae49790ab82053. This tests whether its current early-onset, broad-finish prediction transfers to an unsampled ratio.

The matched m167 20/1, 100 ul condition is predicted at only 2.49/16.56, substantially earlier and narrower than selected m166. Measured m167 anchors 34a133db8364fd665ae6 and fa6fd34875fdc7acf6c1 constrain 5/1 and 50/1 behavior. The pair tests graph-specific beta-diketone transfer and the predicted local onset minimum.

Measure m182 at 10/1 and 100 ul, predicted at 6.14/34.34. Its measured 5/1 reference d7603686249e1fb69a60 already has a broad finish. Together with the selected 50/1 point, this tests whether rigid fluorenone topology supports independent finish growth beyond the behavior of related fused ketones.

Extend the fixed-loading m182 pair to 50/1, where CW distance is approximately 0.993 and the prediction is 9.00/45.56. Related measured fused ketones a36291cab664852df5e5 and 52348febee6695107c49 show different endpoint responses under similar conditions. This label can distinguish topology-dependent tail growth from excessive transfer of late-onset behavior.

Measure m45 at 10/1 and 100 ul between its low-ratio evidence and the measured 20/1 condition e6605c23fb1943a6b848. The 50/1 record 129036e0bccc4ff7e848 has reversed, near-zero endpoints and cannot establish a physical retention trend. This neighboring label anchors the acid's response without treating that record as a reliable solvent-response endpoint.

Introduce molecule-novel m65 at 10/1 and 100 ul. Its predicted onset decreases relative to the supplied 2/1 prediction, while finish increases. With the selected 50/1 point and the related measured ketone anchor 4c10cf623fbb8793829f, this tests transfer to a meta-fluorinated propiophenone.

Complete a fixed-loading m65 ratio pair at 50/1, predicted at 10.15/23.31 with CW distance approximately 0.890. Two labels on this new graph can distinguish a genuinely shallow ketone response from extrapolation error and provide more transferable supervision than two nearly identical loading rows.

Introduce molecule-novel o-tolualdehyde m145 at 10/1 and 100 ul. Measured aldehyde references c6d5f62b278d39ee2c4f and 8b06ec38a7e5999edfa6 provide context, although their PE loading solvent differs from this DCM condition. The selected within-molecule ratio pair will constrain response without attributing all cross-scaffold differences to substitution position.

Measure m145 at 50/1 with the same loading as its selected 10/1 point. The predicted change from 7.63/24.04 to 18.63/35.68 tests whether this previously unlabeled aldehyde follows the model's distinct onset and finish slopes, improving transfer across common aromatic carbonyl structures.

Introduce molecule-novel m93 at 50/1 and 100 ul. This methyl alpha-bromo ester is closely related to the ethyl ester family anchored by 381a7717cd8db0a06c69. Its moderate 9.54/13.68 prediction tests whether small ester substitutions transfer correctly in the weak-eluent regime, complementing the more strongly retained carbonyl examples.

Introduce molecule-novel methyl-substituted bromoanisole m111 at 20/1 and 100 ul. The bromoanisole observation b02cec6868294241a59c uses the same ratio, sample volume, loading solvent, and solvent volume. This provides a close structural transfer test for adding a ring methyl group, with the recorded density difference retained.

Introduce molecule-novel bromochlorotoluene m137 at 1/1 and 100 ul as the lower-ratio anchor for its selected 50/1 condition. Measured halogenated aromatic reference 3e9cbdb1e890c7998372 supplies context. The pair establishes this graph's own response before relying on transfer from other halogen substitution patterns.

Measure m137 at 50/1 with loading fixed to its selected 1/1 point. Its predicted 7.25/13.06 tests weak-eluent transfer in an HBA-free aromatic family where measured examples such as ed12f38d160ee5f34afd and 63ec73e3341feaaf43ae show differing high-ratio behavior. Those references have different loading conditions, so the within-molecule contrast is essential.

Introduce molecule-novel p-diiodobenzene m157 at 1/1, 50 ul with 900 ul DCM. This anchors the selected 10/1 condition at identical loading. The graph is absent from measured data, and the unusually large loading-solvent volume makes an internal contrast especially useful for interpreting structural transfer.

The matched m157 10/1 condition predicts onset near 0.93 mL, compared with 5.08 at the selected 1/1 condition, despite the weaker mobile phase. This is an untested model behavior, not a measured failure. Measuring both points can resolve whether the onset minimum is supported and improve early-elution calibration for heavily halogenated graphs.

Introduce molecule-novel bromopropylbenzene m1 at 50/1 and 100 ul. Its chloro analogue is measured under closely comparable PE loading conditions in ff36ed72f76515960408. The predicted bromide endpoints, 8.04/11.42, test whether halogen substitution transfers correctly while accounting for the associated density-times-volume amount change.

Measure m187 at 5/1 and 50 ul to extend the recent 150 ul observation 5b418229a22585501bfc into a controlled loading contrast. Together with the selected 10/1, 50 ul point, this can determine whether the measured finish decrease from 5/1 to 10/1 is shared across amounts.

Complete the lower-loading m187 ratio pair at 10/1. At 150 ul, measured finish changes from 15.49 in 5b418229a22585501bfc to 10.08 in 108c776e90a5913e6dd3, whereas current predictions for the selected 50 ul pair are much flatter. This discriminates a repeatable condition interaction from an isolated local pattern.

Measure m81 at 5/1 and 100 ul between observed 50 and 150 ul rows 904c7849feb1c686924a and a9500e468002e41eceeb. Their onsets are similar, but finishes differ from 18.80 to 9.23 mL. The midpoint tests whether finish changes systematically with amount or whether one observation is atypical.

Extend m191 to 10/1 and 100 ul, predicted at 21.18/57.88 with CW distance approximately 0.999. Measured 2/1 and 5/1 references 53becf1a41d72abcc45a and 316b7260106904f99ae8 establish substantial finish growth. This label tests continuation of that response for a dialdehyde with historical finish underprediction.

hypotheses.content: Increasing PE/EA weakens the mobile phase, but the magnitude and shape of the retention response depend strongly on scaffold. Interior ratio labels remain useful for identifying curvature and transitions that a universal solvent correction cannot represent.
hypotheses.why_it_matters_for_model_learning: Scaffold-specific response slopes and curvature affect many candidate rows and both prediction heads. Controlled ratio pairs can improve interpolation and structural transfer after retraining.
hypotheses.next_discriminating_question: Do the selected m60, m65, m145 and m74 conditions support the predicted response slopes, or reveal localized changes that require graph-dependent corrections?

hypotheses.content: Sample amount and loading-solvent volume can associate with different changes in onset and finish. Several current local predictions appear too insensitive to these recorded conditions, although irregular observations prevent assuming a single smooth or causal loading law.
hypotheses.why_it_matters_for_model_learning: Matched contrasts can prevent amount and loading-solvent effects from being absorbed into molecular or mobile-phase features. Endpoint-specific contrasts also teach when V1 and V2 should respond differently.
hypotheses.next_discriminating_question: Do the new m125 volume contrasts and m135/m81 amount midpoints support systematic condition effects, or expose isolated observations that should not be generalized?

hypotheses.content: Finish behavior requires supervision beyond onset: substantial V2 errors can remain when V1 is accurate, and broad elution intervals depend on scaffold, ratio and loading. A broad predicted quantile span does not establish either a broad physical interval or a likely measured error.
hypotheses.why_it_matters_for_model_learning: These labels can correct finish and interval-width behavior without unnecessarily moving the onset head. They also test whether recent finish repairs transfer across loading and neighboring ratios.
hypotheses.next_discriminating_question: Once onset is locally constrained, do the selected m94, m166, m187 and m191 labels support the predicted finish response?

hypotheses.content: Detailed topology and functional-group environment may determine when retention-response information transfers between related molecules. Similar aggregate polarity or a close fingerprint match is insufficient to assume equivalent behavior; loading differences must also be retained when comparing scaffolds.
hypotheses.why_it_matters_for_model_learning: New graphs and internally controlled ratio pairs test whether the learned representation shares information appropriately across common ketone, aldehyde, ester and halogenated aromatic families.
hypotheses.next_discriminating_question: Which selected analogue pairs support transfer of response slopes, and which require distinct graph-dependent behavior after recorded loading differences are considered?

hypotheses.content: Some high-PE records have nearly coincident, reversed or near-zero endpoints. They may represent a condition-dependent response or isolated measurement/recording effects; the supplied evidence does not establish physical band narrowing or its cause.
hypotheses.why_it_matters_for_model_learning: These records generated large endpoint errors or violate the expected endpoint ordering. Neighboring labels can constrain how far their behavior should influence amount curves and related structures, although they cannot independently certify reproducibility.
hypotheses.next_discriminating_question: Do the m127 and m57 endpoint patterns extend to neighboring amounts and ratios, and does the adjacent m45 condition support a coherent response around its problematic high-ratio record?

feedback_interpretation: Recent feedback strengthens the case for separate finish supervision: 668279c54bbf75e86496 had essentially correct V1 but a 7.67 mL finish underestimate at acquisition; 0fca9e0134ba9700cc0c, b66aa101a244885dd587 and f72a0e7948a50ed09024 also had substantial finish underestimates. Conversely, 83326d8b972b1f3325e4 and e0bc96df35be6f6a3f05 had overestimated finishes, so broad predictions alone are a weak acquisition rationale. The nearly coincident endpoints in a3ae677aae8a8faf5786 and 63ec73e3341feaaf43ae weaken any expectation that weak eluent necessarily preserves a broad interval; this batch explicitly tests their neighboring conditions without declaring the narrow intervals physical findings. The m187 outcomes motivate a loading-by-ratio contrast because measured finish decreases between 5/1 and 10/1 at 150 ul. Earlier m125 and m135 observations continue to justify controlled loading experiments. I also correct two prior descriptions: higher PE/EA means weaker mobile phase, while 0/1 is neat EA; m127 is o-methoxyacetophenone, not an aldehyde. Historical errors are acquisition-time evidence, not current residuals.
batch_rationale: The batch concentrates labels where they can discriminate between competing explanations. The m127 and m57 contrasts investigate unusual endpoints; m125, m135, m81 and m187 test recorded loading relationships; m94, m166/m167 and m191 constrain finish behavior; and m60, m182 and the molecule-novel analogue tests examine structural transfer. Several experiments form fixed-loading ratio pairs, while others fill a missing point within an existing measured series. The novel low-to-moderate-retention aromatic and ester examples complement the late carbonyl and alcohol regions, helping calibration across the Row-distribution. Duplicate candidate tuples are not selected together. Expected value comes from learning relationships shared by other rows, rather than from maximizing retention or choosing experiments with apparently favorable chromatography. Missing measurement context and irregular repeated observations remain limits on mechanistic attribution.
